etymology: From Middle Dutch splitten, to split or cleave. The older English senses — to divide lengthwise, to rend, to break into parts — are those Webster gave in 1828. The slang sense — to leave, to depart, especially quickly ("Let’s split") — is American and was current in jazz and beatnik talk by the 1950s; it passed to the teenagers of the late 1950s and on into the 1960s. The picture is of a group splitting apart as one member goes his way.
biblical_def: When a teenager of 1957 said "Let’s split," he meant nothing worse than "Let’s go" — the malt shop is closing, the movie is over, time to head home. The older sense is still inside it: a split is a parting, one piece going one way and one the other. Scripture has a great deal to say about leaving, because whether a man stays or goes shows what he loves. Ruth would not split from Naomi: "whither thou goest, I will go" (Rut 1:16). Demas did: "Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2Ti 4:10). When the crowds left Jesus after a hard sermon, He turned to the twelve and asked, "Will ye also go away?" (Joh 6:67), and Peter answered for every believer since: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life" (Joh 6:68). There is a right time to leave — Joseph fled from sin, and a young man should split from a bad crowd before it closes in. But the deepest comfort in the word is what God will never do. Christ does not split on His people: "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5). Grandchildren can say "Let’s split" on the way out of the diner without a care; they should also learn to ask, before they walk out on a friend, a church, or a promise, whether they are leaving like Orpah or staying like Ruth.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (jazz and beat talk, 1950s) for to leave or depart — grown from the 1828 sense of dividing or parting asunder, and a reminder that the Lord who said I will never leave thee does not split on His people (Heb 13:5).
webster_full: SPLIT, v.i. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beat talk) To leave; to depart, especially quickly or together. "This party’s dead — let’s split."

Webster (1828) — SPLIT, verb transitive 1. To divide longitudinally or lengthwise; to separate a thing from end to end by force; to rive; to cleave; as, to split a piece of timber; to split a board. 2. To rend; to tear asunder by violence; to burst; as, to split a rock or a sail. 5. To divide; to break into discord; as a people split into parties. SPLIT, verb intransitive 1. To burst; to part asunder; to suffer disruption; as, vessels split by the freezing of water in them.
Decode for families: when Grandpa said "let’s split," he meant "let’s go" — nobody was breaking anything.
scriptures: Rut 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
Joh 6:67
Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away?
Joh 6:68
Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.
For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: A harmless word for going home; the only caution is that the habit of splitting easily — from friends, churches, and promises — is the very thing Scripture warns against.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing is wrong with split as a way of saying "let’s go." It is breezy and a little cool, and that is all. The word does carry, though, the spirit of an age that was learning to leave easily: to drop out, to move on, to walk away from whatever had grown dull. The 1828 word meant a rending, and leaving is sometimes exactly that.

Scripture prizes the one who stays. Demas split; Ruth did not. Paul begged the church "that there be no divisions among you" (1Co 1:10), and that is the old sense of split — a church torn into factions. A Christian family can enjoy the slang and still teach the older lesson: leave the malt shop when it closes, but keep faith with people.
roots_summary: Middle Dutch splitten (to cleave) → English split (to divide, to rend) → 1950s jazz and beat slang (to leave) → teen and 1960s everyday use.
roots_lines: Middle Dutch splitten — to split, to cleave
16th c.–: English split — to divide lengthwise; to rend; to break into parts
Figurative: a split — a division in a party or a church
1950s jazz and beat slang: split — to leave, to depart
Late 1950s–60s: everyday teen use ("let’s split")
usage: "The jukebox quit at eleven, so we paid for the malts and split."
Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life (Joh 6:68).
I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee (Heb 13:5).

etymology: From Old English thræd, a fine twisted cord, from a verb meaning to twist. The slang threads — clothes, especially sharp ones ("nice threads") — is American, recorded by the 1920s, and was common in the jive talk of the 1940s and the teen talk of the 1950s. It names a suit by the stuff it is woven from.
biblical_def: In 1952 a young man with new threads had a sharp outfit — a two-tone jacket, pegged trousers, maybe a skinny tie — and he wanted everyone at the dance to notice. The word is a cheerful one: it calls clothes by the stuff they are woven from. Scripture takes clothes seriously, because the first clothes were made by God Himself. After the fall, "did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them" (Gen 3:21) — a covering for shame, provided by a death. Jesus told His disciples not to fret over their threads: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin" (Mat 6:28), and yet Solomon in all his glory was not dressed so well. Peter told Christian women that true adorning is not "putting on of apparel" (1Pe 3:3) but "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4). The best threads of all are given, not bought: "he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10). That robe is Christ’s own righteousness, put upon the sinner who trusts Him. So a grandfather can admire a grandson’s new threads and then tell him what Paul told the Colossians to put on: "kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness" (Col 3:12). Those never go out of style.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (recorded by the 1920s; jive and 1950s teen talk) for clothes, especially sharp ones — from the 1828 thread, the fine cord of which cloth is woven, and a reminder that the best garment is the robe of righteousness (Isa 61:10).
webster_full: THREADS, n. pl. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; jive and teen talk) Clothes, especially a sharp outfit. "Dig those threads — is that a new suit?"
Decode for families: "nice threads" means "nice clothes"; the 1828 thread is still in Grandma’s sewing box.
scriptures: Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: A cheerful word with nothing wrong in it; the only caution is the old one about clothes — dressing to be admired rather than to be modest and grateful.
corruption_paragraphs: Threads is honest slang: clothes are made of thread, and the word says so with a wink. There is no oath in it, no mockery, no lust. The young man who wore new threads to the Saturday dance was usually doing what young men have always done — trying to look his best.

The caution is not in the word but in the heart. Clothes can become a way to be noticed, envied, or desired, and Scripture says plainly that adorning should be inward first (1Pe 3:4). A Christian family can enjoy good threads, thank God for them, and remember that He clothes the grass of the field and will much more clothe His children (Mat 6:30).
roots_summary: Old English thræd (twisted cord) → English thread → 1920s American slang threads (clothes) → 1940s jive and 1950s teen staple.
roots_lines: Old English thræd — a fine cord, from a verb meaning to twist
English thread — the yarn of which cloth is woven
1920s American slang: threads — clothes
1940s jive and 1950s teen talk: "nice threads," "new threads"
usage: "He showed up at the sock hop in new threads — charcoal slacks and a pink shirt."
Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin (Mat 6:28).
I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God (Isa 61:10).

etymology: From Middle English thight, dense, close-packed, from a Scandinavian root; the 1828 senses are close, compact, firmly held. American slang has borrowed the word more than once (it meant drunk by the 1830s, a separate sense); the sense "close, intimate," of friends — "those two are tight" — is recorded by the mid-twentieth century and was at home in 1950s talk. The picture is of a knot pulled so tight it will not slip.
biblical_def: When a boy of 1955 said he and his buddy were tight, he meant they were close as two fingers — they rode bikes together, sat together at the ballgame, and would stand up for each other in the schoolyard. That is one of the oldest good things in the world, and Scripture tells its finest story. After David killed Goliath, "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1). That was tight: a king’s son who risked his father’s anger to protect his friend. Proverbs puts it plainly: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17). It also warns that the friends we are tight with will shape us: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). The best of it is that the Lord Jesus calls His people into that same closeness: "Henceforth I call you not servants… but I have called you friends" (Joh 15:15). He is the "friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24), and He proved it by laying down His life for His friends. A grandfather can tell a grandchild: be tight with good friends, and be tightest of all with Christ.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s) for close, intimate, of friends ("those two are tight") — from the 1828 sense of close and firmly held, and a picture of the friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24).
webster_full: TIGHT, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Close in friendship; inseparable. "Jimmy and Bob are tight — you never see one without the other."

Webster (1828) — TIGHT, adjective 1. Close; compact; not loose or open; having the joints so close that no fluid can enter or escape; not leaky; as a tight ship, or a tight cask. 3. Sitting close to the body; as a tight coat or other garment. 6. Close; parsimonious; saving; as a man tight in his dealings. [In common use in America.]
Decode for families: "we’re tight" means "we’re close friends" — not stingy, and not anything worse.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
corruption_summary: A good word for a good thing; the only caution is that a tight circle can harden into a clique that shuts others out, or bind a young person to the wrong crowd.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in tight as a word for friendship. Close friends are a gift of God, and the Bible honours them. The word does have an older slang cousin that is not so wholesome — tight once meant drunk — and families should know the difference, but the 1950s sense is clean.

The cautions are two. A tight group can become a closed one, where outsiders are mocked and newcomers frozen out; Christ’s friendship is the opposite of a clique, for He received sinners and ate with them. And being tight with fools is dangerous, however warm it feels (Pro 13:20). Teach children to choose friends who will make them wiser, and then to be the kind of friend Jonathan was.
roots_summary: Scandinavian root (dense) → Middle English thight → English tight (close, firm) → mid-20th c. slang (close friends).
roots_lines: Scandinavian root — dense, close-packed, watertight
Middle English thight → tight — close, compact, firmly fixed
1830s American slang: tight — drunk (a separate sense)
Mid-20th c. slang: tight — close in friendship ("those two are tight")
usage: "Grandpa and his Army buddy stayed tight for sixty years — Christmas cards every December."
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity (Pro 17:17).
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly (Pro 18:24).

etymology: From English un- (not) and real, from Latin realis (actual, belonging to things). In 1828 unreal meant simply not real, unsubstantial. The slang sense — so good it is hard to believe, amazing ("That car is unreal!") — is American and belongs to the mid-twentieth century; it was in the mouths of 1950s teenagers and has never quite left. The word praises a thing by saying it seems too good to exist.
biblical_def: A teenager in 1958, looking at a new Corvette or the first color television on the block, would say "That’s unreal!" — meaning it was so good it hardly seemed possible. The Christian smiles at that, because the gospel is the one thing in the world that sounds unreal and is the realest thing there is. When the women came from the empty tomb and told the apostles that Jesus was alive, "their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not" (Luk 24:11). Even when the risen Lord stood before them, "they yet believed not for joy, and wondered" (Luk 24:41) — it was too good to be true, and it was true. That is the pattern of God’s works: "it is marvellous in our eyes" (Psa 118:23). The things God has prepared for His people are beyond anything a teenager could dream: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1Co 2:9). Paul says the unseen things are the lasting ones: "the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal" (2Co 4:18). The Corvette rusts. The resurrection stands. A grandfather can tell his grandchildren: when something seems unreal, give thanks — and save your loudest "unreal" for the empty tomb.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s) for amazing, too good to believe — turning the 1828 sense of not real on its head, and a reminder that the resurrection seemed unreal to the apostles and was the realest thing of all (Luk 24:41).
webster_full: UNREAL, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Amazing; beyond belief; wonderful. "Did you see that catch? Unreal!"
Webster (1828) — UNREAL, adjective not real; not substantial; having appearance only.
Decode for families: "unreal" is praise, not doubt — it means "so good I can hardly believe it."
scriptures: And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not.
And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered, he said unto them, Have ye here any meat?
This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.
But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
corruption_summary: A harmless word of wonder; its only weakness is that it spends its amazement on cars and ballgames, and it can teach us to call the most real things the least believable.
corruption_paragraphs: Unreal is exaggeration of the friendly kind, the same family as far-out and awesome. No one who said it meant to deny anything; they meant to praise. There is nothing to correct in it.

There is something to notice, though. A generation that says "unreal" of a new car may come to feel that the spiritual world is the unreal one — that heaven, the resurrection, and the judgment are pious tales. Scripture turns that around (2Co 4:18). The seen is passing; the unseen is solid. A Christian can use the slang freely and still teach that the most amazing things God has done are not unreal at all.
roots_summary: Latin realis (actual) → English real → unreal (not real, 1828) → 1950s slang (amazing, too good to be true).
roots_lines: Latin res, realis — a thing; actual
English real — actually existing; true
unreal — not real; unsubstantial
1950s American slang: unreal — amazing, beyond belief
usage: "Dad brought home a hi-fi and played his records so loud the windows shook. Unreal."
Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard (1Co 2:9).
And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not (Luk 24:11).

etymology: Of uncertain origin; American slang of the mid-twentieth century, plainly modelled on the older wet blanket (a person who smothers fun, as a wet blanket smothers a fire, in use since the nineteenth century). A wet rag is limp, damp, and no use at a party: the killjoy, the bore, the one who will not dance.
biblical_def: In 1954 nobody wanted to be the wet rag at the party — the fellow who sat in the corner, sighed at the music, and said it was time to go home before anyone else was ready. The word is teasing rather than cruel, and it carries a real truth: a sour spirit dampens everyone around it. Scripture agrees. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones" (Pro 17:22). God does not want His people gloomy; He commands joy: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice" (Php 4:4). When Israel wept at the reading of the law, Nehemiah told them to stop and feast, "for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). But Scripture also guards the quiet person from the mockers. Some who look like wet rags are carrying a grief no one sees, and to push cheer on them is cruel: "so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart" (Pro 25:20). The Christian way is better than the party’s way: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). Christ Himself wept at a grave and went to a wedding. A grandfather can teach both lessons at once — don’t be a wet rag, and don’t call the sad one a wet rag either.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (mid-century, after the older wet blanket) for a killjoy or a bore — a word with a true warning about sour spirits and a needed caution, for some who seem dull carry a heavy heart (Pro 25:20).
webster_full: WET RAG, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; compare wet blanket) A killjoy; a dull, spiritless person who spoils the fun. "Come on, don’t be a wet rag — one more song."
Decode for families: a wet rag is the one who puts out the fun — but check first whether he is bored or hurting.
scriptures: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Php 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
Neh 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
corruption_summary: A teasing word with a true warning against sourness, but it can turn into mockery of the quiet, the sober, and the grieving.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a fair point in wet rag. A believer who is always sour, always complaining, always the last to laugh, is not showing the joy of the Lord, and Scripture calls him to cheer up (Php 4:4). Grandparents who used the word often meant it kindly: come on, join in.

The danger is in the other direction. The name was also thrown at the boy who would not drink, the girl who went home early, the one who would not laugh at the dirty joke. Scripture calls that sobriety, not dullness. And some who sit in the corner are grieving; there is "a time to weep" (Ecc 3:4). A Christian should be slow to call anyone a wet rag and quick to ask what is wrong.
roots_summary: wet blanket (19th c., one who smothers fun) → wet rag (mid-20th c. American slang) → a killjoy, a bore.
roots_lines: wet — soaked, damp; rag — a limp scrap of cloth
19th c.: wet blanket — one who smothers fun as a blanket smothers a fire
Mid-20th c. American slang: wet rag — a killjoy, a dull or spiritless person
Kindred words: drag, square, party pooper
usage: "Everybody was dancing but Harold. What a wet rag."
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine (Pro 17:22).
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep (Rom 12:15).

etymology: A rhyming jive greeting, current in the 1940s and still heard among 1950s teenagers; it was popular enough to give its title to a 1943 Hollywood musical. Buzz is imitative, the hum of bees; it also came to mean a low murmur of talk or a rumour, and the greeting asks, in effect, "What’s the talk? What’s new?" Cousin here is not kin; it is chosen for the rhyme and the friendliness.
biblical_def: "What’s buzzin’, cousin?" was the bright, rhyming hello of the jive era — a sailor on leave in 1944, a soda jerk in 1951, anyone who wanted to sound hep. It meant "How are you? What’s new?" and the person greeted was no more a cousin than the moon. Scripture is full of greetings, and they are better than ours. Boaz walked into his barley field and said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee" (Rut 2:4). The risen Christ came to frightened disciples behind shut doors and said, "Peace be unto you" (Joh 20:19). Paul closed his letters with greetings by name. A greeting is a small act of love; it tells a person he is seen. The question in the jive phrase is also worth answering well. The buzz of the world is mostly rumour, and Christians are told to starve it: "where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20). But there is news worth passing on: "As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Pro 25:25). And the best answer to "What’s buzzin’?" is the oldest good news there is: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings" (Isa 52:7) — Christ is risen, and He saves sinners.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (a rhyming jive greeting of the 1940s–50s) for What’s new? How are you? — from the 1828 buzz, a whisper or report spread secretly, and an invitation to pass on good news rather than rumour (Pro 25:25).
webster_full: WHAT’S BUZZIN’, COUSIN?, phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; jive) A rhyming greeting: What’s new? How are you? "Hey, Eddie — what’s buzzin’, cousin?"

Webster (1828) — BUZZ, verb intransitive 1. To make a low hissing sound, as bees; to make the sound of z, with an expiration of breath between the tongue and the roof of the mouth or upper teeth. 2. To whisper; to speak with a low hissing voice; to make a low hissing sound. BUZZ, verb transitive To whisper; to spread, as report, by whispers, or to spread secretly. BUZZ, noun The noise of bees; also, a whisper.
Decode for families: it is just "hi, what’s new?" — the cousin is only there for the rhyme.
scriptures: Rut 2:4
And, behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said unto the reapers, The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee.

Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
corruption_summary: A cheerful, harmless greeting; the only caution is that "the buzz" can mean gossip, and a Christian should pass on good news, not rumour.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong in this greeting. It is friendly, silly, and musical, and it made people smile. Rhyming hellos like it (see you later, alligator) were the play of a generation that had come through a depression and a war and wanted to laugh.

The one thing to watch is in the word buzz itself. A buzz is a murmur passing from ear to ear, and the buzz is often gossip. When a friend asks what’s buzzing, a Christian can decline to pass along the rumour (Pro 26:20) and find something better to share — a kindness, a prayer answered, the good tidings of the gospel.
roots_summary: Imitative buzz (the hum of bees) → a murmur, a rumour → 1940s jive greeting "What’s buzzin’, cousin?" → 1950s teen hello.
roots_lines: buzz — imitative of the hum of bees
buzz — a low murmur of talk; a rumour passed along
cousin — kin, here used only for the rhyme and the warmth
1940s jive: "What’s buzzin’, cousin?" — What’s new?
Kindred rhymes: see you later, alligator
usage: "Grandpa still greets the mailman with ‘What’s buzzin’, cousin?’ and the mailman grins every time."
As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country (Pro 25:25).
Peace be unto you (Joh 20:19).

etymology: A rhyming phrase of 1950s teen and jive talk, of uncertain origin. The word had long meant the real news or the latest information ("What’s the word?"); adding from the bird made it rhyme and made it sound like inside news straight from the source. Compare the older saying "a little bird told me."
biblical_def: "That’s the word from the bird" meant, in 1956, "This is the real story — you can count on it." Teenagers passed it along about the dance, the test, or who was going steady with whom. Behind the slang sits an old idea that Scripture got to first. Solomon warned that secrets fly: "a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter" (Ecc 10:20). What you say in private has a way of getting out, so say nothing you would not want carried. But the phrase also points to a deeper need: everybody wants the straight story, and most of what flies about is not. "The words of a talebearer are as wounds" (Pro 26:22). There is one word that is never second-hand and never wrong. "Every word of God is pure" (Pro 30:5). Jesus prayed for His disciples, "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" (Joh 17:17). And unlike the news at the malt shop, it does not go stale: "the word of the Lord endureth for ever" (1Pe 1:25). A grandfather can teach his grandchildren to be careful which bird they believe, and to know where the true Word from above is found — in the Book, and in Christ, the Word made flesh.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (a 1950s rhyming phrase) for the truth, the straight story — echoing the old warning that a bird of the air shall carry the voice (Ecc 10:20), and pointing to the one Word that is always true (Joh 17:17).
webster_full: WORD FROM THE BIRD, phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) The truth; the straight story; reliable inside news. "No school Friday — that’s the word from the bird."
Decode for families: it means "this is the real scoop" — no actual bird involved, though Solomon would say be careful anyway.
scriptures: Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
corruption_summary: A playful, harmless rhyme; the only caution is that "the word" at school is often gossip, and the phrase can give rumour an air of authority it has not earned.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no sin in the phrase. It is a rhyme for fun, like many from the same years, and it often carried perfectly true news — the game was moved, the teacher was sick.

The caution is that the "word from the bird" was also how rumours travelled, and the rhyme made them sound certain. Scripture asks for honest speech: let yea be yea (Mat 5:37). A Christian can enjoy the phrase and still check his facts before he passes them on, and keep the word truth for what has been proved.
roots_summary: "What’s the word?" (the real news) → 1950s rhyme "the word from the bird" → the straight story; compare "a little bird told me."
roots_lines: the word — long used for news, report, or the latest information
"a little bird told me" — an old saying for news from a secret source
1950s American slang: word from the bird — the truth, reliable inside news
Kindred rhymes: what’s buzzin’, cousin?
usage: "Coach says practice is off tomorrow — and that’s the word from the bird."
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth (Joh 17:17).
Every word of God is pure (Pro 30:5).

etymology: American, of uncertain origin; hot diggity and hot diggity dog are recorded from the 1920s as nonsense exclamations of delight, built on hot dog!, itself an exclamation of the same kind. Perry Como’s 1956 hit "Hot Diggity (Dog Ziggity Boom)" carried it into the Silent Generation’s young adulthood. It is a pure noise of joy, with no oath hidden in it.
biblical_def: "Hot diggity!" was what a boy in 1950 said when his father came home with a puppy, or when school was let out for snow. It is a noise more than a word — the sound of joy bubbling over. Unlike some exclamations of those years, it hides no sacred name; it is simply glad. Scripture has room for gladness out loud. "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing" (Psa 126:2), the psalmist says of the day God brought the captives home. The shepherd in Christ’s parable who found his lost sheep did not keep it quiet; he called his neighbours and said, "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost" (Luk 15:6). That is a hot-diggity moment, and Jesus says heaven has the same joy over one sinner who repents. The Christian difference is only this: joy should know where it comes from. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights" (Jas 1:17). So the puppy, the snow day, and the ballgame are all reasons for "Hot diggity!" and for thanks. "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it" (Psa 118:24).
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, recorded from the 1920s; a 1956 hit song) for an exclamation of delight — a pure noise of joy with no oath in it, and a fit companion to the shepherd’s Rejoice with me (Luk 15:6).
webster_full: HOT DIGGITY, interj. (American slang, 1920s–50s; also hot diggity dog) An exclamation of delight or excitement. "Hot diggity! No school tomorrow!"
Decode for families: it means "Hooray!" — a happy noise, nothing more.
scriptures: Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them.
Luk 15:6
And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
Php 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
corruption_summary: A wholesome exclamation with nothing to correct; its only lesson is that joy should turn into thanks to the Giver.
corruption_paragraphs: Hot diggity is one of the clean exclamations of its era. It does not borrow God’s name, as gee and golly do, and it does not curse. It is nonsense of the happy kind, and grandparents who still say it are teaching, without meaning to, that you can be loud and glad without being profane.

The one thing a Christian can add is the object. Gladness that stops at the gift misses the Giver (Jas 1:17). A family that says "Hot diggity!" over a snow day can also say grace over it, and teach children that rejoicing in the Lord (Php 4:4) is the deepest kind of hot diggity there is.
roots_summary: hot dog! (early 20th c. exclamation) → hot diggity (dog) (1920s) → 1956 popular song → Silent Generation exclamation of delight.
roots_lines: hot dog! — early 20th c. American exclamation of approval
1920s: hot diggity, hot diggity dog — nonsense exclamation of delight
1956: a popular song carries the phrase to a new generation
Kindred clean exclamations: swell, neat, yippee
usage: "Hot diggity! Dad says we’re driving to the Grand Canyon this summer."
This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it (Psa 118:24).
Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost (Luk 15:6).

etymology: From Old English blæst, a blowing, a gust of wind. The older English senses — a gust of wind, the sound of a trumpet, a blight, the explosion of powder — are centuries old; Webster’s 1828 verb meant to blight, to strike with a loud blast, or to split rocks with powder. The slang sense — a wild party or a great time ("We had a blast") — is American and recorded by the 1950s, from the idea of an explosion of fun. It became one of the most durable words the Silent Generation passed down.
biblical_def: When a girl came home from the church hayride in 1957 and said "We had a blast," she meant they had laughed all the way there and sung all the way back. It is a good thing to have a blast, and Scripture does not frown on it: God "giveth us richly all things to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17), and there is "a time to laugh… and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4). The older word reminds us who owns the real blast. In the Bible a blast is God’s breath or His trumpet. At the Red Sea Moses sang, "with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together" (Exo 15:8). At Jericho the walls fell at a long blast of the ram’s horn (Jos 6:5). Fun is a gift, but it makes a poor god. Solomon tried to live for it and found it empty: "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2). Paul warned of a day when men would be "lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God" (2Ti 3:4). So a grandfather can say both things: have a blast, children — laugh, sing, play ball till dark. But keep the fun in its place, under God, and remember that one day the last trumpet will sound its own great blast, and those who love Christ will enter a joy that never ends.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s) for a great time or a wild party ("we had a blast") — from the 1828 blast of wind or trumpet, and a word Scripture lets us enjoy under the God who giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1Ti 6:17).
webster_full: BLAST, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A great time; an exciting party or outing. "The church hayride was a blast."

Webster (1828) — BLAST, verb transitive [Literally, to strike.] To make to wither by some pernicious influence, as too much heat or moisture, or other destructive cause; or to check growth and prevent from coming to maturity and producing fruit; to blight, as trees or plants. 2. To confound, or strike with force, by a loud blast or din. 3. To split rocks by an explosion of gun powder.
Decode for families: "had a blast" means "had a great time" — no explosives, and no cursing (the old exclamation blast it! is a different use).
scriptures: Exo 15:8
And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together, the floods stood upright as an heap, and the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Ecc 2:2
I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;
corruption_summary: A cheerful word for a good time; the only danger is the old one of loving pleasure more than God, or calling a sinful party a blast.
corruption_paragraphs: Having a blast is not a sin; Scripture gives us laughter, feasts, and dancing in their season. The word itself is clean, and most of the blasts our grandparents remembered were picnics, dances, and road trips.

The caution is twofold. First, fun can become a god, and a life arranged around the next blast is the life Paul described (2Ti 3:4). Second, the world often calls a blast what God calls drunkenness or lust; the word can dress up sin as a good time. A Christian family can have a blast together and still teach children to ask whether the fun is the kind they could thank God for.
roots_summary: Old English blæst (a blowing) → English blast (gust, trumpet sound, blight, explosion) → 1950s slang (a great time) → lasting everyday English.
roots_lines: Old English blæst — a blowing, a gust, a breath
English blast — a gust of wind; the sound of a trumpet; a blight; an explosion
Biblical: the blast of God’s nostrils (Exo 15:8); the ram’s horn at Jericho (Jos 6:5)
1950s American slang: a blast — a great time, a party
usage: "We drove to the shore in Uncle Ed’s Buick, eight of us crammed in. What a blast."
A time to weep, and a time to laugh (Ecc 3:4).
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice (Php 4:4).

etymology: From duck, the bird, used as a term of endearment in English since Shakespeare’s day ("my duck," "ducks"); ducky as an endearment followed. American slang turned it into an adjective meaning fine, delightful, or just right, current in the 1930s and 40s. By mid-century it was as often said with a wink: "Oh, that’s just ducky" meant the opposite.
biblical_def: In 1946 "everything’s ducky" meant everything was fine — the boys were home, the ration books were going away, the kitchen smelled of pie. Later the word got a sly twist, and "Well, isn’t that just ducky" meant something had gone wrong. Both uses touch a question Scripture answers well: how does a Christian say "everything’s fine" and mean it? Paul could say it in prison: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11). That is not pretending; it is trusting. "But godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6). David looked at his lot and said, "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage" (Psa 16:6). And Habakkuk, with the fig tree bare and the stalls empty, still sang, "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation" (Hab 3:18). The sarcastic "just ducky" is the opposite spirit — a complaint dressed as a compliment — and Paul has a word for it too: "Do all things without murmurings and disputings" (Php 2:14). A grandfather can teach both: say "ducky" when it is ducky, and when it is not, take the trouble to the Lord instead of to sarcasm. In Christ, even a hard day can be well with the soul.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (from an old English endearment; American use in the 1930s–40s) for fine, delightful, just right — later often sarcastic, and a doorway to the contentment Paul learned in every state (Php 4:11).
webster_full: DUCKY, adj. (American slang, 1930s–40s; often ironic later) Fine; delightful; just right. "The picnic went off without a hitch — everything was ducky."
Decode for families: "ducky" means "fine" — unless Grandma says "just ducky" with raised eyebrows, which means the opposite.
scriptures: Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
Psa 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
Hab 3:18
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
Php 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
corruption_summary: A sweet, harmless word; the only fault comes in its sarcastic use, where "just ducky" becomes murmuring with a smile.
corruption_paragraphs: Ducky comes from a term of endearment and has kept some of that warmth. Said plainly, it is a happy, slightly old-fashioned way of saying all is well, and there is nothing in it to correct.

Sarcasm is another matter. "Isn’t that just ducky" is grumbling in disguise, and Scripture counts murmuring as a real fault (Php 2:14), the sin of Israel in the wilderness. A Christian family can keep the sweet use and drop the sour one, and practise saying honestly, "This is hard, and the Lord is good."
roots_summary: duck (the bird) → duck, ducks (term of endearment) → ducky → American slang adjective (fine, delightful) → ironic "just ducky."
roots_lines: duck — the water bird; from Old English
English endearment: my duck, ducks, ducky — dear, darling
American slang, 1930s–40s: ducky — fine, delightful
Mid-century irony: "just ducky" — said when things go wrong
usage: "Mother set the turkey on the table, the whole family was home, and everything was ducky."
But godliness with contentment is great gain (1Ti 6:6).
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places (Psa 16:6).

etymology: American, of uncertain origin; the picture is of a high, bald forehead like the top of an egg, the stock cartoon of a professor. The word is recorded earlier in the century, but it came into wide use in the early 1950s as a mocking name for an intellectual, and that decade gave it its lasting sting.
biblical_def: In 1953 an egghead was the bookish fellow with thick glasses and a big vocabulary — the kid who read during recess, or the professor on television whom nobody quite understood. The word was half a joke and half a sneer. Scripture cuts both ways here, and a grandfather should too. First, against the sneer: learning is a good gift. "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom" (Pro 4:7). The Bereans were praised for searching the Scriptures, and Paul asked for his books and parchments in prison. Mocking a child for loving to read is no virtue. Second, against the pride the word sometimes caught: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1). Head-knowledge without the fear of God is only cleverness, for "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" (Pro 1:7). The rulers of Jerusalem were eggheads of a kind, and they marvelled that Peter and John were "unlearned and ignorant men" who spoke so boldly — then "they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus" (Act 4:13). There is the answer to both the sneer and the pride. In Christ "are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3). The smartest child and the slowest one sit at the same feet.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American; widespread in the early 1950s) for an intellectual, often mocking — a word that warns against both sneering at learning and being puffed up by it, for knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1).
webster_full: EGGHEAD, n. (American slang, widespread 1950s) An intellectual; a bookish or highbrow person, usually said with a mocking edge. "Ask the egghead — he’s read every book in the library."
Decode for families: an egghead is a brainy person — and it is kinder to say "smart" than to say it with a sneer.
scriptures: Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
corruption_summary: A mostly playful word that carries real mockery of learning, and sometimes a hint of the pride that learning without God can breed.
corruption_paragraphs: Egghead was often said with affection, but just as often it was a put-down, a way for the crowd to punish the child who was different. Scripture does not let us despise any gift God gives, and a love of learning is one of them. To mock it is the scorner’s way; Proverbs pictures scorners who delight in their scorning while fools hate knowledge (Pro 1:22).

The word also caught a real fault: the clever man who looks down on plain folk. Knowledge puffs up (1Co 8:1), and some eggheads did deserve to be taken down a peg. The Christian answer is not to mock either the scholar or the farmer, but to bring both under the fear of the Lord, where learning becomes humble and the humble learn.
roots_summary: egg + head (high, bald forehead) → American slang egghead → early 1950s wide use (an intellectual, mocking).
roots_lines: egg — from Old Norse; head — from Old English
Cartoon image: the high, domed forehead of the stock professor
Early 1950s American slang: egghead — an intellectual, often mocking
Kindred words: brain, highbrow, later nerd
usage: "They called him an egghead in school; now he’s the doctor who set my arm."
Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1).
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Pro 1:7).

etymology: American, of uncertain origin; recorded around the turn of the twentieth century for a strikebreaker or a company spy, and then for any informer. By the 1950s it was a schoolyard word for a tattletale or a contemptible heel, and a verb besides (to fink on someone); later it was doubled as rat fink. Proposed sources, such as German Fink (a finch), remain unproven.
biblical_def: In 1955 the worst thing you could be in a schoolyard was a fink — the kid who ran to the teacher, the one who told. The word means an informer, and by extension any low, untrustworthy person. Scripture helps a family sort out what is wrong and what is not. Talebearing is wrong: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" (Lev 19:16), and "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter" (Pro 11:13). The Bible’s great informer is Judas, who went to the priests and asked, "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?" (Mat 26:15). Betraying a friend for gain is real wickedness. But not all telling is finking. When Paul’s nephew heard of a plot to murder the apostle, "he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul" (Act 23:16), and saved his life. A child who tells a grown-up that someone is in danger is not a fink; he is a friend. And Jesus gave a better path for ordinary wrongs: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone" (Mat 18:15). Grandparents can teach both halves: don’t carry tales, don’t sell out a friend — and don’t keep quiet when someone is being hurt. Christ was betrayed by a friend for thirty pieces of silver, and still He laid down His life for sinners of every kind.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, from about 1900; a schoolyard staple of the 1950s) for an informer or a contemptible person — a word that rightly condemns talebearing and betrayal (Lev 19:16) but wrongly shames honest telling.
webster_full: FINK, n. (American slang, c. 1900; schoolyard word 1950s) An informer, a tattletale; a contemptible person. Also v., to fink on. "Don’t tell Mom — don’t be a fink."
Decode for families: a fink is a tattletale or a heel — but telling a grown-up when someone is in danger is not finking.
scriptures: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.
And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
And when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul.
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
corruption_summary: A word that names a real sin — betrayal and talebearing — but is also a weapon of contempt and a pressure to keep silent about wrongs that ought to be told.
corruption_paragraphs: Fink is an insult, and Jesus warned about contemptuous names: "whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council" (Mat 5:22). Raca names an empty, worthless fellow, and fink is close kin to it. A Christian should be slow to call anyone by it.

The deeper problem is the code behind the word. The schoolyard rule "never tell" protects bullies as often as friends. Scripture forbids talebearing and betrayal, but it never forbids telling the truth to someone who can help (Act 23:16). Families can teach the difference plainly: tattling for spite is wrong; speaking up for the weak is right.
roots_summary: Of uncertain origin → American fink (c. 1900, strikebreaker, informer) → 1950s schoolyard word (tattletale, heel) → later rat fink.

1950s schoolyard: fink — a tattletale; a contemptible person; to fink on
Later: rat fink
usage: "Somebody finked on us about the broken window, and we all got detention."
A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter (Pro 11:13).
